blocks.x: . All right, so the name, please.

My name is Dr. Edmar Suchaw, and I'm speaking from 523 Betts Place, Matary, Louisiana, which is a little suburb right outside of New Orleans. I was born in New Orleans October 25, 1897. Still going strong, I hope.
When did you first become aware that there was such a form of music as New Orleans?

Well, my introduction to it was many, many years ago. I don't think I was aware of it as being jazz, nor was it called jazz then, but I had a nice, a Negro nice, who used to take me walking up and down St. Charles Avenue, and occasionally, a mother would let me accompany her to the grocery, which was in the Negro section about five squares away from St. Charles Avenue towards Dryad Street. And it was amazing how she seemed to get by grapevine that every time we went to this grocery, there'd always be a funeral procession with a marching band. And I didn't know what it was all about, but it enthused me very, very much. And I loved to join in a bunch of both whites and Negro children that were following the band along the street. And it happened to be that I was listening to Joe Oliver at that time. That was my introduction to it.
Well, what did your parents think of this whole music? And your parents...

Well, of course it didn't enter into anything at all. And when the marching parades happened, funeral parades, Negro processions happened to pass, they'd always come out and look at it, and listen with enjoyment, but with a tongue-in-cheek attitude towards it. My next real introduction to music, if you will, I had a grandmother who sang and played very well. My father, she sang and played the piano and accompanied herself. And my father played the guitar a little bit. He also played an alto horn. But when I was nine years old, my grandmother decided that I should play a guitar and bought me one. And they hired a very lovely lady, I remember her name, Miss Casnavette, to give me lessons. And after three lessons, she told my family I was perfectly hopeless. It was no use to persist. I was wasting their money and her time. So the guitar got put aside for about two, three years. And then the neighborhood where we lived, there was the Greenmire family, the Hanes, the Downwinds, the Frelson Pages, Esperberto, and several fellas right nearby. The mothers got together and decided that we should have a neighborhood dancing class. And I had to have a terrible spanking to make me go to the thing. I had no idea of having anything to do with girls at all. But once I got there, first thing I ran into was a trio, a piano, drums, and a bass fiddle, who now I know were playing ragtime, because I still remember the tune. It was a lizard on the rail. They call it his Hiawatha, Red Wing. And from then on, they had no trouble making me go to dancing school. But I didn't dance a doggone bit. I'd just sit around and listen to the music until the teacher made me come up and do one or two steps with her. And from then on, if there happened to be a band with a guitar in it, I would always hang around watching the musician playing it and then go home and try. Then we had a group of fellas about my age, maybe 12, that finally discovered that secretly we were each trying to play string instruments. So we finally got together and began practicing every Sunday afternoon at the home of Mr. and Ms. Robert Reynolds on Marengo in Pretania. And we finally got proficient enough until we'd call on different girls on Sunday afternoon, the whole band, which was seven or eight of us. And for sandwiches and Cokes, we'd play a whole evening. And that part was quite acceptable to everybody concerned because it was not loud music. It was all strings, violins, sometimes two violins, banjo, two guitars, bass fiddle, and a mandolin.
Well, what type of music did you end up playing? The popular music of the day or...?

Yes, but it was jazzed up. I have some examples of that. You see, of that group, which was originally seven men, four of us still play together. And a band that was at that time in its infancy became known as the six and seven eight string band. It was, became very popular and we even played for the Queen of the Carnival's Supper dance at the Stratford Club Mardi Gras Night. We had gone up to twelve. We could bring in some ringers and increase the band up that much.
And what year was that that you played?
Mm-hmm. I wasn't any more than fifteen years old then. And that was definitely...
That was 1912.

A form of jazz music that you were playing? It was definitely not ragtime, I can tell you that. It was my interpretation of the difference between jazz and ragtime is, if you'll put it as simply as possible, is one is jerkier than the other one. And let's say the same difference that there is between jazz and swing, there is between ragtime and jazz. It was a smoother type of the same sort of music. But then our interest in the music became very deeper, much deeper personally, not with any idea of analysis. I wasn't... We didn't know anything about style. We didn't know anything about the various musicians, except we knew them by their names. And we danced enough by them to... them to know us. We knew Oliver. We knew Ori, Dodds, Johnny and Baby Dodds, Clarence Williams, A.J. Pierron was a great, great, had a great band. And for many years, they were the top society band. And then Robichaud did a great deal of the society stuff too. He also played at Louisiana, which is now Diamond Jim Moran's place, but it was a magnificent, well-run restaurant in those days and they had wonderful parties. But when was this? That was from 1914 up to the outbreak of World War I. And then after the war, it resumed again. Those bands were all readers. They were not... They were wonderful musicians. We had Lorenzo Teo on clarinet, who still goes down in history, one of the greatest clarinets. He was with Pierron. And Pierron also had a fellow by the name of Steve Lewis on piano, who was, I think, the model from which Fats Waller got so, you know, most of his great stuff. And then there was a drummer by the name of Louis Cottrell, who is credited with being the first drummer who introduced the press role into the music. But these people were playing society music and they couldn't really blow that top in real rat-gut barrel-house jazz. Now, Robichaud, who was this left-hand... Both Negro bands, light Negro, was a left-hand violinist, and he had a society orchestra too. But he always included a hot... One hot man in it who'd take off on choruses. But the straight reader would predominate all the way through and they had fine rhythm. Then the real origins of the early white New Orleans bands, the bands that people know as the original Dixieland Jazz Band, the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, didn't exist at all, in fact, in New Orleans, until they went away from here and started recording them. They had to make up a name and they assumed those names. But I knew all those men individually and the bands were continually changing, interchanging musicians and personalities. And in that way we were about their age, maybe they were a few years older, but we would sit there and listen very much. Then we'd go home and try to play the same thing on string instruments. The attitude of the older folks, I remember my father saying that when he was a young buck around 18, they had one of the slaves that was called Snowball. He was as black as the Ace of Spades, who always was brought in to play piano, totally uninstructed, but he said he played ten-fingered piano that they danced to, the Schottish and the Maezurka and all those old-time dances. He said he was magnificent. The attitude, of course, was that he was an entertainer and there because he was a fine musician and had good rhythm. But there wasn't any idea of a leveling process through the music or a consideration on anything but a hired person that they paid for. Even the slaves got it or paid if they did something special like that. I can't go on without another question of some kind.
Well, let's get back to the social aspect of it for the world in society. When you first started going to parties, they tend to have Negro bands or jazz bands or white or colored.

I think that there was... I very seldom remember white bands playing until 1915 or 16. Then a few of them made inroads on the Negro bands. That was Tom Brown's band, Happy Shilling's band, Bud Fisher's band, and the Detroit boys who played over Cobb's restaurant. They were a strictly white band and they also played on the outside. Johnny and Paul Detroit.
Well, did these Cobb bands and white bands both play?
They never played together, but they all were playing jazz music, which was still not known as jazz music yet.
Well, what did adults in that day think of it? And what did you and your friends think of it?

Well, for one thing you must remember, that there was no radio or television at all. The movies were silent movies. And we had to afford a great deal of our own entertainment, which came through the string instrument. And the families were always for that because it kept us together and they knew where we were and all that. And outside of the music gradually bringing us into places that were questionable, which we didn't always tell them where we had been, the attitude was they were glad to see us play it. And, but to ever consider following a career as a musician was probably damned to perdition, especially a jazz musician.
Well, did they think the music itself had any value as music?

They didn't consider that at all. It was just something for them to dance by. As for listening to records, I think it annoyed them to listen to that type of records. In fact, in New Orleans, I think you'll find, aside from the race records, it sold to the Negro population, which was comparatively late when they discovered that there was a fine market. It was 19, probably 18 or 19, before the real race records came out. And then they weren't even put in the white music shops, like Green Walls and Well Irons. Not that they were advised to them, because they had no sale among the white people.
And the race records were, of course?
They were strictly for Negroes, and they sold like hotcakes there, a very big market among the Negro population here.
And that was strictly?
It was all Negroes, both singers and players on those records.
Well, then you would say that your parents' contemporaries didn't see too much value for the music itself.

I don't think they understood it at all. It had a very definite beat, and the dancing steps were quite simple in the earlier days, although I remember before we finished college that with the days of coming to Charleston and all that stuff, they became quite complex. But always, never the dancers, I hope that works. This one, it is. Anyway, the dancers always, bodies were touching, and they never pulled away from each other to permit freedom of the feet. And there had to be perfect synchronization of the two dancers, the partners. And for that reason, there was a rather slow tempo, which permitted the limitations of the anatomy of the human to gyrate and to keep step. Although it did pick up and get, there's one step, in other words, you would take one step to the bar, and it was quite slow. And the two step was supposed to be very complicated when it came out. But the two step is a, if my memory serves me right, was a, fitted in very well with ragtime, idiom at the time. Now, as for the older people's attitude towards the, let's say, I'm trying to see how that social question comes up, because it never did occur in our mind as to having anything that would be considered on a social scale, either as an acceptance, as an art that started here, or a form. Many times the bands were, made the old folks rebel because they played too loud. They were accustomed to playing in halls, and you'd get them in a home, and they'd blast everybody out of the place. And I think that's one of the things that they, they objected to. Then the, another thing, there was no distinction in this way, that a musician who was hired for the evening, be white or colored, would not mingle with the guests at all. If he was fed, he'd be fed in the back, even in a private little dining room or an anteroom or in the kitchen, you know. And that went for the whites and the negroes.

Well, uh, going through your early days, could you tell me, uh, you said that, well, the, uh, jazz music was used a lot for parties, for private parties off of big dances of some sort, and it was accepted as big music to have? Yes. And, uh, that...

And there, there were not always big bands. There may be a single piano, or a piano with rhythm, or two or three string instruments, and then it gradually grew into five and then into seven. But that required the larger homes to have a full band. Well, uh...
Say, when you were in high school, your high school was dancing, was it normal to have a jazz band? Oh, yes. What about in college? Well, at Tulane, the... How many years that you were there?

The gymnasium, yeah. I was in Tulane in 1915. I started, but the war broke out in 16, and I left. And I came back in 19, I think, or 18, and started over. But already they were having... When we were seniors in high school, they were having script dances at the Tulane gym on Saturday night for a dollar a couple. They had nothing but a big pool of ice water at one end, no refreshments. But this, what is now used is, I don't think it's... It's next to the Tulane gym on the campus now. Was it... Do you know which building I'm talking about? It was the... It was the... formerly the Tulane gymnasium. It was further... Uptown and downtown. Further towards Broadway. It was Howard Tilton Library, which is right next to it.
Maybe I'm wrong.
Maybe it's on the other side, but... Maybe ROTC building. What do they have in there now? Maybe ROTC.
Are they sleeping quarters now? I really don't know. I doubt they're sleeping quarters now, unless maybe for the offices.

Well, it could be that, but they had always the finest jazz bands in the city available at that time. Joe Oliver was the most popular band of all, and I remember going down into the old district where he was playing in Storyville to hire him to go for those dances. It was from 8 to 12, and that was it, unless they took up a... Pass the hat and got enough money to keep them to one o'clock, and that was the limit.

Well, do you think you could, as closely as possible, trace the... Use of jazz bands for entertainment from then down to now, and also the interest in it as a form of music, and the attitude of white New Orleans...

Well, I still think that today, in your audience, in spite of a very remarkable awakening within the past 10 years, which is due to the younger generation suddenly discovering jazz and accepting it, that in the old folks' mind, it still has nothing of value. It's probably degrading, and... It wasn't spoken of in polite society as anything but a nigger band for dancing. Now, as far as the type of bands, I remember that Irene Castle came to the St. Charles Hotel in around 1920, and Pierron was playing there, and she begged him to come on a tour. They were a white couple, and he refused. He was perfectly satisfied here. But that was not... Although I loved the band and the music, and I knew many of the men intimately, it was not real New Orleans music. It was more of a polished idiom, much closer to swing than the real jazz. Now, as for the real rough bands, Ori used to have his own band, and we weren't so crazy about him, because Ori himself blew the most foul trombone you ever heard. He never did blow right on the note. The older he's gotten, the more he's improved, particularly since he's on the West Coast. Now, Armstrong, who was just the kid coming up at the time then, we never hired him unless we were absolutely broke and couldn't get anybody else because he blew false, and he blew too loud, and he was a rough, rough character in his youth. Now, the... I'm trying to see the thread that I started out. The young kids that would give their own dance at Tulane insisted on using the finest real, authentic jazz bands. But that was then, all from the time I was in early high school, all through college. And then what happened in New Orleans in 1916 or 1917 when World War I broke out, they closed up Storyville, which was a restricted district, and many of the found musicians moved to Chicago. But I'm very much at variance with the opinion of so many of the so-called jazz authorities who live away from here and spend a week or two weeks in New Orleans and then go home and write a tome about all they know about jazz. Because I think that, in my personal opinion, and the little research that I have done on it, less than five, and if I give 10%, I'm being very generous, less than 10% of the musicians ever even played in Storyville. They probably got the best recognition on account of that. But many of them, many of the particularly fine white bands would not go down there. It was not only a very low area, it was a very dangerous area. It was shooting and cutting. It was vicious. But coming back to the real authentic Negro bands, there was the Silver Leaf, there was Celestin, there was the Columbia, there was the Eagle, there was the Gold Leaf, the Maple Leaf. Those were all Negro bands and they were offshoots of the marching bands who would also break it down to just five or six to furnish dancing music. And the more polished big parties always had white bands which, even if they played jazz, they'd tone them down. That was later on as the 20s were coming on. But many of these Negro men who played in these bands worked as doormen and butlers and waiters and cooks, and then supplemented their income with their music.

Well, do you think you could, in some sort of chronological order, carry down from, say, 1920 to the present, the use of a white society of jazz bands for entertainment and also the recognition given to it as a value?

Well, I can talk a little bit about that if you'll be patient with them by trying to pose them as an authority because I've gotten a great deal of much more pleasure out of it than anyone would dream. But when I tell you that I have been the only one in your audience who's done any research at all up to right now, and the two men that the Hogan has selected with the Ford Foundation couldn't have been better selected, but neither one of them are Orleanians. And I couldn't name you another real Orleanian born and bred here that has had any interest besides me. It's been a lonesome one-man stand. And whenever I talk on the subject, I bring out the fact that the attitude of the New Orleans public has been tolerance and acceptance, and more as a minstrel entertainment that provided a fun or a good beat. But when I quoted on the phone to you, the attitude of the upper crust, even now, they have still that feeling of let's put on a tuxedo and go slumming, let's go down to the French Quarter and hear some of the bands. They still don't know what it's all about. I don't think they want to be bothered either.
In general, when you say that white New Orleans still has no appreciation of...

I would say there's a very limited clique, which you're beginning to find out already, I'm sure, of the jazz cult. That's just as much of a fraternity as Beta or Sigma Chi or anything else. You have entree almost any place in the United States if you know yourself about jazz. I don't say you get into the inner sanctum. It's certain you'll be led so that you can meet the right people for it. In your audience, I have been very kind. I've spoken before combined history classes of Tulane. I've spoken to the Fine Arts Club at Loyola. I've spoken before the Library Society. Twice before the Round Table Club. Once before the entire student body of Sophie B. Wright High. And the Executive Club and the Cooperative Club at the Roosevelt. And I've been invited as a guest to Lenox, Massachusetts when they have their annual meeting at Music Inn up there, which lasts about a month. And I've talked before the invitation of the Florida State University last year. The year before last, I spoke at the Ringling Museum of Art. And without dwelling on the subject too much about the social side, I stressed more what the music meant and where its origins came from. And I think your approach to this subject is one that's brand new in your audience. And I think you're doing something quite valuable. I don't see, however, how you can do it in two weeks.

And this is just a small paper. It's just a term paper. Yes, I think. A lifetime could be devoted to it. But I'm just, but I'm seeing experts in the field like you. I'm also seeing people that like it. Whether you have to go out of their way or to hear it. Just people with casual interests. Also people that hate it and despise it. I'm just trying to get a general picture of what New Orleans have thought of it through the years.

You'll find a few exceptions among the intelligentsia who would like it and want to go hear it. Even without considering they're doing something wrong or away from the beaten path. But they don't know what they're listening to. And they have no desire to fraternize with it or get on better terms with it at all.
And you said that is a majority?

I would say the vast majority if I had to put it to... I think most everybody in your audience likes jazz. There are very few that don't. But as for accepting it, let's say this, that you even... If you're going to analyze the thing that I would say the general public is more accepting it more than the upper crust. The middle and law classes would accept it. It's their music, the law people, the law classes. That's where it came from. That's one of the forms of entertainment that cost nothing and that it was theirs. It came stemmed from a desire to do something, to be creative, and they had their own fun with it. And it still goes on that way.
What would you consider as the upper crust?
I mean the people who are executives, who are probably in the social register, or in the higher income brackets. And let's include also the underpaid teachers at the colleges and schools.

In other words, you would include us in the upper crust of New Orleans. In other words, when I speak of New Orleans, the middle and upper classes, the people would go to debut art parties. Sure, sure. The members of New Orleans, the challenges of two ways. That's correct.

That's correct. You know what I call the middle and upper classes, you call the upper crust. Well, I said, when you say the upper crust, I mean a very limited few. Well, I'm not looking into just a limited few.
I mean from the very top down to some...

I'd say from the, let's say, middle classes, which takes in a very larger number now than ever before. People that are well behaved and soft spoken, some education, regardless of background or extraction, they're the coming America. And they have to be considered in this discussion. And I think their general acceptance is much more than those that are highly trained or specialized in any line. Coming back to the social side, they say the blue noses, blue bloods.

Well, in summer then you could say that New Orleans throughout the years have used it as a form of entertainment for... used jazz as a form of entertainment for music, I mean for dances and such like. They would, uh, some of them value in it as music, for instance, as they were thinking in, you see, in Beethoven or Bach. That would say, nobody, for the most part, would see any value in the music, but, uh, except as entertainment. And as entertainment was used, it has been used widely. Would you say that?
I think that's true.
What about, uh, the use of it as entertainment? Uh, really, the years, they tend to fall off during the 30s with the national dance theater.
Oh, as far as jazz was concerned. Paul Whiteman and that type of band did more to destroy. In fact, it's...
I don't even call... I'm a semi-purist. I don't call, uh, Whiteman a swing or progressive, even jazz. For me, jazz just means that... Well, you are a pyrist.
...the music originated by New, by New Dominions. Well, I think you are a pyrist.
And that's not, that's the subject of mine.

Well, I, I feel that, uh, the, uh, other types of music, the men, they came on with the augmented bands, and the strict arrangements that cracked the style of the real, authentic musician like Muggsy Spanier playing in all these big bands, or Big Spider-Beck completely lost in the Whiteman outfit, that, that completely... jazz, you could come in, couldn't find a jazz band for 15, 20 years.

Well, uh, is that true in New Orleans? I mean, the, the normal small, say, three to, to eight pieces, the usual seven piece, six, six, seven piece, real, as good as jazz bands. Were they used, did the use of those tend to fall off during the, during the 20s of doing a duty?

They didn't play at all. Yeah, they had a hell of a time, and gave, finding a band to engage. There were one or two that continued, uh, um, Celestan kept a group fairly well together, although they didn't play very often. They were available. Uh, who else besides Celestan? There were two or three other Negro bands that were available, but, uh, you had nowhere to get them, and you had to go hunting for them. Now, there were small restaurants and, uh, places like Marmaloo's out at the lake there. Have you ever been to that place? No, it's not happening. Well, uh, out at Littlewood's, if you've ever been there, these places that go out over the water, some of them are restaurants. And they used to have on Friday or Saturday nights, when they'd have a big play for seafood, then they'd have a little archaic jazz, the real old-time Negroes that would play there.
But you said that, listening to these bands, you'd hang up for parties, almost die out completely for a while. And by what period would that be?
Oh, when Swing was king, wherever that was, I would say, beginning from the late 20s, uh, all the way through up to 1945. And during that period, up across New Orleans...
They danced to the bigger bands. And, and, and, most of them didn't know that such existed, or that, uh...

I think they were only too happy to, uh, to exclude it from their minds. One of the things that, even though I am a purist and love, uh, I think, New Orleans music, I can't understand why so many of the Negro bands will continue to, uh, blow so many bad notes. They, they, they, discards mean nothing to them. As long as they're hell-bent for leather with a fine drive to the thing, and it's very thrilling and exciting, they still blow a lot of bad chords. And they make no attempt to, to, uh, learn them or to correct that. And I think that was one of the big offending elements to the people that did know music. A bad tone or an instrument that was out of tune or a discard, they couldn't take it. So...
Were any of the discards intended as the defilences of a professor or...?

I don't think, I don't think they thought that. I think that, uh, the, uh, authorities, uh, and let's say, I'd name two that are, uh, backtracking in their early theories. Marshall Stern, whose book I love very much, uh, and Rudy Brush. I think both of them are backtracking on their... One of their statements was that Johnny Dodds purposely tuned his clarinet a little bit flat, because he said it gave the effect, and this is quoting Glish, of a sort of an acrid sound that was similar to vinegar in a salad. Vinegar itself you wouldn't like, but combined with the whole business, it gave it a tang. And that is dead wrong, because they were, first of all, playing with four instruments that were either retrieved from ash cans or second-hand stores. Uh, and, uh, they couldn't get the damn thing in tune, or their ear wasn't attuned sufficiently. And I think that's one of the things that the people who did know something about music objected to, is the dissonance that was unpleasant. Uh-oh! Sorry. Well, in the summer then you could say that, unless we were only in the 30s, uh, then...

I assume that in the sense of the... the...the environment were interesting... the real stuff in the 30s, uh, I mean in the 40s, the middle 40s, early 40s came along, uh, a chap by the name of Scoop Kennedy, who is now connected with WDF, D-F-F-TV, who is an authority on cooking.

Well, when the 30s, I mean in the 40s, the middle 40s, early 40s came along, a chap by the name of Scoop Kennedy, who is now connected with WDSU-TV, he's an authority on cooking. He was a guiding light in the formation of the National Jazz Foundation, which promised to be a very great thing. And we had chapters all over the world, and it was a little Mimicraft magazine that didn't amount to too much. His secretary put it out. But they had some of the greatest concerts down here, sponsored by Esquire. We had the winners of all the Esquire contests that would come down here, and we had a national hookup where we had, imagine this band down here. James B. Johnson on piano, Pops Foster on bass, Johnny Dodds and Zully Singleton all mating on drums, J.C. Higginbottom on trombone, Roy Armstrong, Sidney Bechet.
Sidney Bechet actually returned to New Orleans?

Oh, yes, he came back then. He was here for a good while. He's not so mad against New Orleans. He was fed up on Chicago when he walked out of the Jazz Limited out there. But that was, we had, that was among other things. We dug up as many of the old original Dixieland jazz band, and they put them on the stage out there. We had Bunk Johnson's marching band on the stage. But the winners of this individual award were this band that was here. On the West Coast was Duke Ellington, who had won the band, whole band contest. And in New York was Benny Goodwin, who had won the clarinet contest. So when we went on the air, after an individual broadcast, first from New York, then from New Orleans, and then from the West Coast, the finale was they all put on headphones, and Benny blew his part into this mic up there, and it mixed with the front line here. And in California, Duke Ellington accompanied that front line. It was a fantastic setup. Well, that lasted about three or four years, and it blew up. The war came along again. The real war. World War II. No, World War II. And Kennedy left the organization, went to Europe in charge of YMCA entertainment over there. And there was nobody over here who was able to take over in his place, and the thing folded.
Well, that was organized in the late 30s?

No, that was organized in the early 40s. Oh. Then in 1948, when New Orleans Jazz Club came into being, and we've been going 10 years now. We've had some very fine concerts, and I really, without patting ourselves on the back, believe that two-thirds of the old musicians that are playing again today are due to our efforts of taking them up.
Maybe like Papa Salister?

No, he was still playing, but he played any number of concerts for us. And Eddie Pearson's group, Paul Barbarine's group, George Lewis's group. That's talking about nothing with the Negroes. Shock, it was Steve Adorn on the room in front. And we dug him up. And Harry Shields, who was Larry's brother, he was running a diesel engine at night on a switch engine, LNN, and so on down the line, one after the other like that. And we just finally get together and play and jam, bring him up to the club, and finally we gave some concerts. And Hip Ginley read one and saw the possibilities, and then he put Sharky into the famous store, and he was there for five straight years. And then all the rest of them built up. The paddock picked up Salister. And right across the street, El Marocco, which is now a striptease joint, had George Lewis. At his best. He had Elmer Talmud with him. Part of that band would roll when he was playing. And so on down the line. Well, uh... Now, what I don't understand is the stupid thing of people sitting around listening to jazz. I don't know why in the hell they don't dance to it. Same thing, but... The musicians would prefer it. They get a great kick out of seeing the sympathetic reaction of the people. And it's boring to everybody concerned to just sit around and listen. I think that the people who do that ought to play pop, progressive. Then you can be the so-called cerebral music lovers where nobody has any fun. It's sad music. Well, uh... What about, uh...
Since the... The Bible of the... Small bands, what about the use of them at private parties?
Well, I think you find that more and more now.
I think there's...
Not only the, uh... Union bands, both Negro and white, but there's any number of young bands that are coming up. And that's one of the things...
They play the old... Oh, yeah.

As close as they can. Uh... One of the points that I brought up, and I wrote a chapter for Eddie Condon's book that's coming out soon. Uh... It's an evaluation of the situation of jazz music in New Orleans.
